scale: 4 Arabic dialects, multiple evaluation tasks (MC QA, short-answer, multi-turn dialogue)
key_metric: TLoRA outperforms full-network LoRA, zero-shot, and few-shot on Arabic medical QA and clinical dialogue

title: Agents Catching Agents: Shortcut Cascades and Benchmark Gaming in Clinical Multi-Agent Systems

Referee oversight: 77-88% precision, 13-21% FPR — transfers across modalities
Near-silent gaming: only 1/10 text and 1/134 imaging drifters name the moved-toward rubric

dataset_size: 7 cohorts, 6 public datasets spanning text, imaging, and tabular ICU records

title: CARE-Bench: Benchmarking Patient-Facing LLM Triage

Prompting improves to 46.9-63.4 but substantial threshold errors remain
Only 33.5% of prompted outputs preserve 'ask for more info' step

models_evaluated: 11 LLMs under unprompted and prompted open-ended protocols; GPT-5.5 mapper

TiTrATE / GRACE-3 / Bárány Society frameworks used to construct ED dizziness vignettes
Quantifies magnitude of bias with 95% confidence intervals vs neutral control

title: Benchmarking Language Models for Clinical Safety: A Primer for Mental Health Professionals.
authors: Flathers M, Nguyen PA, Herpertz J, Granof M, Ryan S

title: Beyond Accuracy: A Mixed-Methods Audit of Chain-of-Thought Failures in LLM-Based COVID-19 Vaccine Stance Detection.
authors: Praschk A, Fischill-Neudeck V, Caspari T, Wiesinger HP

title: RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning

title: A corpus-specific clinical RAG system matches or outperforms newer frontier LLMs on HealthBench

title: AI in cardiovascular care — systematic review and meta-analysis of 31 RCTs (n=1.69M patients)
authors: Ong AQC, Ang CS, Bojic I, Johnson CL, Aggour H, Ng FS, Car J, Leeson P, Gonçalves J, Lai NM

title: CARE: Confidence-Aware Reasoning for Reliable Medical VQA
authors: Yuetian Du, Yucheng Wang, Zhenyuan Chen, Luyuan Chen, Rongyu Zhang, Jinjian Zhang, Wei Zhou, Zhijie Xu, Ming Kong, Zhan Zhou, Jie Liu, Qiang Zhu
abstract: Reinforcement Fine-Tuning (RFT) has enabled medical Multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) to produce Chain-of-Thought reasoning for visual question answering, yet they suffer from confidence miscalibration — a systematic gap between expressed certainty and actual diagnostic accuracy that undermines clinical trust. CARE is a Confidence-Aware REasoning framework that jointly optimizes accuracy and calibration via dual-stage pipeline (Medical-CoT SFT + GRPO with Confidence-Aware Reward). Across three Medical VQA benchmarks, CARE achieves highest diagnostic accuracy with lowest Expected Calibration Error and Hallucination Rate. (Accepted at MICCAI 2026)
relevance: Methodology for confidence-aware clinical VQA reasoning — directly relevant to clinical AI safety/calibration and OE-style physician-AI teaming at point of care
key_findings: Identifies confidence miscalibration as a systematic gap in medical MLLMs
Dual-stage pipeline: cold-start Medical-CoT SFT + GRPO with Confidence-Aware Reward tying confidence to correctness
Best diagnostic accuracy + lowest Expected Calibration Error (ECE) + lowest Hallucination Rate across 3 Medical VQA benchmarks
Frames CARE as foundation for trustworthy clinical decision support
Code released at github.com/anotherbricki/CARE
Accepted at MICCAI 2026
tools_evaluated: Medical MLLMs (general); benchmarks specific to paper

title: ETHOS: Modular Ethics Framework for Clinical Multi-Agent Systems
journal: arXiv preprint (cs.MA, cs.AI) — Pacific Symposium on Biocomputing 2027 submission
tools_evaluated: Clinical multi-agent systems (generic framework, demonstrated on hepatology MAS)
key_findings: Modular ethics governance meta-agent integrable into any clinical MAS without architecture changes
Layered oversight: deterministic checks + contextual reviews + ethics critic
Improves decision reliability by detecting incomplete, inconsistent, or out-of-scope evidence
Appropriately increases abstention when safe recommendations cannot be supported
Translates high-level ethics principles into deployable, auditable runtime safeguards
relevance: Clinical AI safety governance framework — practical implementation of ethics oversight for multi-agent clinical decision support.

title: Demographic Injection in Medical Language Models under DEI Prompts
tools_evaluated: 47 LLMs across general, medical-domain, open-weight, and proprietary families
scale: 4 medical benchmarks, 376,000 responses, validated model-judge pipeline
key_findings: DEI prompt raises demographic injection rate from 0.7% to 33.1% (47x) in all 47/47 models tested
Effect attributable to equity content, not length (18x above length-matched control, p=1.4x10^-14)
0.25-2.4% of responses: invented demographic changes the answer, 99.8% toward incorrect option
Phrasing scales effect from 14% to 56%
General mechanism: any reasoning nudge can cause unrequested patient detail fabrication
relevance: Large-scale safety evaluation revealing novel failure mode in medical LLMs — demographic hallucination from prompting that can alter clinical recommendations.

title: RareLens: Towards End-to-End Rare Disease Care via Aligning Divergent Large Language Model Reasoning
tools_evaluated: GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro, RareLens ensemble
scale: RarelensBench: 157,525 cases, 33 Orphanet categories, 7,000+ conditions; external eval: 1,287 cases, 23 physicians
key_findings: RareLens outperformed all frontier models (GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1, Claude-3.7-Sonnet, Gemini-2.5-Pro) across all four stages of rare disease care
Achieved AUC 0.917 for screening, top-1 accuracy 65.5% for diagnosis and 89.8% for treatment
Both autonomous RareLens and physician+RareLens outperformed unaided physicians in external evaluation
Divergent model reasoning is an exploitable source of information for clinical AI under high uncertainty

title: Multidisciplinary dental treatment planning by artificial intelligence: A comparative evaluation
authors: Kazim SA, Alnoman BA, Hashim RM, Goodacre CJ
scale: 10 cases, 4 AI systems, 4 calibrated specialists, 5-domain rubric (kappa=0.74)
key_findings: OpenEvidence highest mean score (7.7+/-1.4) vs ChatGPT-5 (7.6+/-1.1), Gemini (5.1+/-1.2), Copilot (4.7+/-3.1)
Copilot failed 3/10 cases due to content filtering
Clinically significant diagnostic errors across all systems - adjunctive use only

title: Vocal Cord Dysfunction: Evaluating the Utility of AI LLMs for Patient Education
authors: Cook K, Tseng P, Ahmadian D, Demirjian N, Liu V, Weinstein T, Yip H
journal: World Journal of Otorhinolaryngology - Head and Neck Surgery
scale: 4 patient questions, 45 provider raters, Friedman + chi-square analysis
key_findings: AI preferred over expert-authored response for definition, diagnosis and treatment-process questions (all Friedman p<=0.001)
ChatGPT 5 Extended Thinking best overall; OpenEvidence comparable on definition question and several items

title: The Role of Large Language Models in Hormonal Contraception Consultation
authors: Psilopatis I, Emons J, Zwimpfer TA
scale: 10 fictitious counseling cases, 2 board-certified OB-GYN raters
key_findings: Accuracy and comprehensiveness of LLM counseling evaluated against evidence-based guidelines across eligibility screening, contraindications, drug interactions, side-effect management and emergency contraception

title: Guideline-anchored RAG outperforms baseline and literature-only configurations in gynecologic oncology decision support: A pre-integration benchmark
authors: Dukes D, Yost C, Wang R, Diagne YF, Garr L, Yost M, Owaka J, York M, Kang P, Sookram J, Huh W, Loaiza A, Farley J
scale: 50 de-identified gyn-onc cases, 3 gynecologic oncologists, modified Generative Performance Score (mGPS)
key_findings: NCCN-guideline-anchored GPT-5 RAG outperformed both baseline GPT-5 and OpenEvidence (literature-anchored) on mGPS
OpenEvidence lacked NCCN guideline access during the study window - literature-only retrieval trailed guideline-anchored retrieval for guideline-driven oncology decisions
Pre-integration benchmark informing health-system CDS procurement

title: Right Diagnoses, Decorative Reasoning: A Perturbation Audit of Medical Chain-of-Thought
authors: Mengzhu Xu, Jifan Gao, Xia Jiang, Yaoxin Wu, Xi Long
tools_evaluated: 14 LLMs (panel including medical and general-purpose models)
scale: 14 LLMs, 4 medical QA benchmarks, 197 clinician-annotated perturbed questions
key_findings: 72.9% Chain-Decoupling Rate — chain does not register clinically meaningful edits and answer does not flip
Chain corruption leaves accuracy unchanged, removing CoT prompting does not reduce accuracy
Pattern holds across medical and reasoning fine-tuning and scale
Two board-certified clinicians confirm 98.5% of gold answers remain defensible after perturbation
relevance: Directly evaluates clinical AI safety by auditing whether chain-of-thought reasoning in medical LLMs is faithful or merely decorative. Introduces the Chain-Decoupling Rate (CDR) as a reusable yardstick. 14 LLMs tested on 4 medical QA benchmarks including MedQA.

title: SDoH-Aware Narrative Anchoring Bias in Medical LLMs for Trustworthy Clinical Decision Support
scale: 300 clinical cases, 8,100 model responses, 3 prompting conditions
key_findings: 31.67% narrative sensitivity error — models change answers when same case written in different patient voice
Qwen2.5 7B: 56.33% accuracy, 40.33% correct consistency
Paired McNemar tests show significant accuracy gains for 7B over 3B in all prompt settings
Trustworthy clinical decision support requires evaluating stability across medically equivalent patient narratives
relevance: Directly evaluates clinical decision support safety by measuring whether medical LLMs change answers based on patient narrative voice rather than clinical content. Introduces narrative sensitivity error metric.

title: Performance of a domain-specific large language model in answering patient questions in psychiatry
authors: Alexander J. Hish, Arjun Nagendran, Scott N. Compton
scale: Patient questions about escitalopram, 10 board-licensed psychiatrists
key_findings: MIND rated highest by rubric in all domains (accuracy, clarity, completeness, nuance, safety, referral appropriateness)
Psychiatrists preferred ChatGPT (57.6%) over MIND (42.4%, p=0.003)
MIND rated more complete than ChatGPT (small effect size, p<0.001)
MIND and ChatGPT rated safe with same frequency (p=0.955)
OpenEvidence included in comparison but not top-rated
relevance: Directly evaluates OpenEvidence alongside ChatGPT and a domain-specific LLM (MIND) in psychiatry. One of the few studies comparing OpenEvidence to other tools in a specific clinical specialty.

title: Teaching LLMs How ICU Physicians Approach Clinical Reasoning Through OMOP-Aligned Retrieval Improves Reasoning Across Clinical Domains
authors: Miguel Contreras, Scott Siegel, Subhash Nerella, Jessica Sena, Jiaqing Zhang, Heng Sun, et al.
scale: 19 clinicians, 5 clinical reasoning benchmarks, 8B-70B parameter models
key_findings: Clin-REACT models outperformed backbone models across 5 clinical reasoning benchmarks
Gains extended to script concordance tests and downstream diagnosis/treatment tasks
Expert ICU reasoning supervision generalizes beyond critical care
19 clinicians contributed to dataset through clinician-in-the-loop framework
relevance: RAG-based clinical AI evaluation — demonstrates that expert reasoning supervision in critical care improves broader clinical reasoning. Directly relevant to OpenEvidence's RAG architecture and clinical decision support approach.

title: Benchmarking Clinical Decision Pathway Adherence in Large Language Models
authors: Nuo Chen, Xinyang Jiang, Zilong Wang, Zhifei Zhang, Xiaoye Qu, Jiajun Deng, Yulan Guo, Cairong Zhao
scale: 42,353 clinical cases from 2,274 English and Chinese clinical practice guidelines
key_findings: MEGA-CDP benchmark evaluates guideline adherence in clinical decision pathways. 16 LLMs tested in single-turn vignette and multi-turn interactive settings. Reliable clinical decision support remains challenging. Introduces CDP-oriented evaluation framework for pathway consistency.

title: A Comparison of the Agreement of Four AI Models on Surgical Recommendations of MIRCTs Using the ASES Neer Circle Delphi Recommendations as a Baseline
key_findings: OE highest concordance with expert Delphi consensus (65-69%). ChatGPT-4o second. DeepSeek lowest. All below expert-level.

title: Physician Ratings and Adoption of AI-Generated e-Consultation Advice: A Randomized Clinical Vignette Study
key_findings: Faculty rated OE advice 4.2-4.7/5. Adoption OR 8.43. Source labeling (human vs AI) had no effect.

title: Reference quality of OpenEvidence across five medical specialties
key_findings: Zero fabricated references across 4979 citations. 3 attribution errors. Most references recent and high-impact.

title: Evolution of Generative AI in Clinical Practice: Comparative Performance of OpenEvidence 2.0 and ChatGPT-4o
key_findings: OE superior citation validity. ChatGPT generated fabricated references. First comparison using cervical spine clinical guideline queries.

title: OpenEvidence errs on the safe side in a structured test of triage recommendations
key_findings: OE conservative triage safety profile. Contrasts with ChatGPT Health 51.6% under-triage rate. Same benchmark.

title: A five-phase evaluation framework for diagnostic and predictive medical artificial intelligence
key_findings: Five-phase framework from lab to clinical benefit. Addresses gap between retrospective testing and real-world deployment.

title: ChatGPT-assisted vs Traditional Teaching of Diagnostic Assessments: RCT
authors: Xu H, Sun Y, Mo ZW
key_findings: Randomized controlled trial of ChatGPT-assisted diagnostic assessment teaching
Comparative evaluation against traditional teaching methods
Medical education AI integration study

title: Comparative LLM Evaluation for Fetal CNS MRI Diagnostic Reasoning
authors: Yu R, Peng M, Li H
key_findings: Head-to-head LLM comparison for fetal CNS MRI diagnostic reasoning
Retrospective diagnostic accuracy study
Multi-model evaluation in radiology context
